theme: God has taken his place in the divine council
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 82. It is a short psalm in which God holds court over the “gods” and condemns them for judging unjustly. Read it slowly, and notice that Jesus quotes it.
settingTheScene: Psalm 82 is a psalm of Asaph. It describes God taking his place in the divine council and passing judgment on those called “gods.” Interpreters differ on who these are: human judges and rulers, or heavenly beings who held authority over the nations. Either way, the psalm’s point is clear: all who hold power answer to the LORD. It pairs with Psalm 58 as a statement of God’s concern for the weak.
observation: “God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment” (v. 1).
“How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked?” (v. 2).
“Give justice to the weak and the fatherless; maintain the right of the afflicted and the destitute” (v. 3).
“Rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked” (v. 4).
“They have neither knowledge nor understanding, they walk about in darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken” (v. 5).
“I said, You are gods, sons of the Most High, all of you” (v. 6).
“Nevertheless, like men you shall die, and fall like any prince” (v. 7).
“Arise, O God, judge the earth! For you shall inherit all the nations!” (v. 8).
interpretation:
The psalm opens in a courtroom in heaven. God is the judge, and those who stand before him are called “gods.” The word elohim in the Hebrew can refer to God, to angels, or to human authorities who act in God’s name. Some read the “gods” as the spiritual powers behind the nations, and others as human judges, called gods because they exercise God-given authority. In either case, the meaning of the psalm is the same. Those entrusted with rule are accountable to the one who rules over all.

God’s charge is about the poor. He does not accuse them of false doctrine. He accuses them of partiality and injustice. The tests of a ruler are: do the weak receive justice? Are the fatherless and the afflicted protected? God lists four things: give justice, maintain rights, rescue, and deliver. These are the duties of anyone with power.

Verse 5 describes the consequence. When rulers fail, “all the foundations of the earth are shaken.” Injustice at the top destabilizes everything. A society that does not protect its weakest members loses its footing.

Verse 6 and 7 are the heart of the psalm. God says that he appointed them: “You are gods, sons of the Most High.” They have a high calling. But they will die like any man. The honor of their office does not make them immortal. The psalm humbles all who hold power.

The final verse is a prayer: “Arise, O God, judge the earth!” When human rulers fail, the psalmist turns to God. He is the only perfectly just ruler, and he will inherit all the nations.

When Jesus was accused of blasphemy for calling himself the Son of God, he quoted verse 6 (John 10:34-36). If Scripture could call mere human rulers “gods” because the word of God came to them, how much more could the one whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world claim to be God’s Son?
connection: Jesus quotes this psalm in John 10:34-36. He is the true judge, to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 5:22). Colossians 2:15 says that Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities. 1 Corinthians 15:24-25 says he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The psalm’s last line is fulfilled in Revelation 11:15: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ.”
application:
If you have authority at work, in your family, or in your church, ask how you treat the weak.

Pray for rulers to remember they will die, and that they answer to God.

Pray “Arise, O God, judge the earth” for a specific situation of injustice.
prayerPrompts: Pray for those in authority to give justice to the weak.
Ask him to keep you from abusing any power you have.
Praise him as judge of all the earth.
